profilePeriod: Conservative leadership and premiership, 1975–1990; earlier votes used as context
scopeNote: Answers are editorial simulations of documented political principles, not a questionnaire completed by the person. Brazil-specific statements are interpreted in the analogous home-country context. Modern hypothetical technologies require inference.

sources.title: UK Government: History of Baroness Thatcher
sources.evidence: Leadership from 1975, premiership 1979–1990, elected governments, Falklands war, privatisation, deregulation, union reform, tax cuts, and market mechanisms in health and education; chemistry education.

sources.title: Thatcher: Bruges speech
sources.evidence: Defended sovereign parliamentary nations, single market and GATT liberalisation, rejected external protectionism, supported NATO and modern nuclear deterrence alongside arms-control negotiation; distinguished free movement of goods from border controls against crime and illegal migration.

sources.title: Thatcher: Scottish Conservative Conference
sources.evidence: Explicitly rejected legislative devolution and defended the Union; described individual ownership and parental school choice as devolution to people rather than politicians.

sources.title: Thatcher: Election press conference on education
sources.evidence: Promised national curriculum and attainment targets, alongside delegation of budgets to headteachers and schools opting out of local authority control.

sources.title: Thatcher: Church of Scotland General Assembly
sources.evidence: Christian morality, family, responsibility, religious education and established Christian heritage; explicitly affirmed democracy, equality under law for other faiths and cultures, and legally guaranteed provision for health, education, pensions, sickness and disability. Christianity does not prescribe one institutional programme.

sources.title: Thatcher: World in Action immigration interview
sources.evidence: Sought sharp reduction and eventual end of immigration with compassionate exceptions; expressed anxiety about cultural displacement, while insisting people already resident be treated equally under law.

sources.title: National Archives: The origins of Section 28
sources.evidence: 1987 conference speech rejected school teaching of an inalienable right to be gay; Section 28 entered the Local Government Act in 1988, restricting local authorities promoting homosexuality.

sources.title: Hansard: Firearms (Amendment) Bill
sources.evidence: Government proposed prohibiting full-bore self-loading rifles after Hungerford; tighter controls on shotguns while retaining sporting weapons. This is government policy, not a quoted personal statement by Thatcher.

sources.title: Hansard: Interception of Communications
sources.evidence: Government defended interception powers for security and serious crime within a statutory framework, with safeguards and individual remedies; not unlimited indiscriminate surveillance.

sources.title: Thatcher: Interview for The Sun
sources.evidence: Favoured restoring capital punishment for exceptionally grave murders, subject to judges; not abolition of courts or trial.

sources.title: Hansard: Bank of England role
sources.evidence: Government explicitly had no plans for a more independent Bank of England, arguing inflation remained elected government responsibility.

sources.title: Thatcher: Speech in Edinburgh
sources.evidence: Pledged not to dismantle the NHS, defended increased real resources, disability support and provision for vulnerable people; distinguishes market reform from abolition of public healthcare.

sources.title: Thatcher: Royal Society speech
sources.evidence: Supported science and technological advance, identified greenhouse warming and ozone threats, and endorsed Montreal limits on CFC consumption.

sources.title: Thatcher: UN General Assembly environment speech
sources.evidence: Advocated nuclear power, scientific research, industrial innovation and continued growth, but binding climate protocols, tropical forest and biodiversity protection, reducing chemical inputs, energy efficiency and pollution controls.

sources.title: Hansard: Clause 11 embryo research
sources.evidence: Thatcher appears among Noes to restrictive amendment and Ayes on clause 11 standing part; context is licensed embryo research. Supports regulated medical research rather than a categorical religious prohibition; does not establish approval of designer babies.

sources.title: Commons Hansard: International Womens Day debate
sources.evidence: Peter Bottomley recalls Thatcher voting for male homosexual decriminalisation and helping pass the 1967 abortion bill. Retrospective parliamentary testimony about earlier votes, not evidence of a changed 2023 position.

sources.title: Thatcher: Daily Mail interview on Grenada and cruise missiles
sources.evidence: Disagreed with the US invasion of Grenada despite the US alliance; guarded sovereignty and questioned overthrowing a government because its ideology was hostile.

sources.title: Diplomatic School library: The Downing Street Years
sources.evidence: Catalogues Margaret Thatcher as author; London HarperCollins 1993; politics and Great Britain subjects; supports original year and authorship.

sources.title: Google Books: The Downing Street Years
sources.evidence: Political memoir by Margaret Thatcher about her premiership; combines contemporary events with argument and political philosophy.

sources.title: Vale de Cambra municipal library: Os anos de Downing Street
sources.evidence: Verified Portuguese title and translation by Artur Lopes Cardoso, Bertrand, Venda Nova. This is a Portuguese edition, not evidence of a Brazilian edition.

facts: 1988 rejection of Scottish legislative devolution.
1987 national curriculum coupled with school budget delegation.
estrutura.tension: Unionist national legislative authority coexists with administrative and individual autonomy; opposition to Brussels centralisation does not make her a domestic federalist.

facts: 1979–1990 elected parliamentary leadership.
1988 explicit endorsement of democracy as safeguard against abuse by the few.
representacao.tension: Strong executive within parliamentary consent; not popular assembly governance or an unelected technocracy. Parliamentary supremacy differs from judicial supremacy.

facts: 1987 supported capital punishment in grave murder cases.
1985 legal interception with safeguards; 1988 government firearms restrictions.
poder.tension: Order and counterterrorism coexist with rule of law and lawful opposition; surveillance positions do not justify inventing unlimited arbitrary detention.

facts: 1978 urged greatly reduced immigration and cultural continuity.
1978 demanded equal treatment of residents and compassionate exceptions; 1988 affirmed tolerance.
imigracao.tension: Restrictive admission and integration differ from ethnic expulsion or blanket rejection of minority religious customs.

facts: 1982 used force to recover Falklands.
1988 NATO, modern nuclear deterrence, and arms-control negotiations.
diplomacia.tension: Strong professional defence and willingness to fight do not imply compulsory service, unlimited nuclear proliferation or rejection of negotiation.

facts: 1988 promoted active NATO commitment including deployments beyond its area.
1983 opposed US invasion of Grenada.
intervencao.tension: Assertive national interests and alliances are bounded by sovereignty and case-by-case judgement, not permanent isolation or automatic regime change.

facts: Privatisation and right-to-buy expanded private ownership.
Defended public NHS and social support while introducing market mechanisms.
economia.tension: Private enterprise is central but police, courts, tax-funded healthcare and a safety net remain legitimate; not anarchocapitalism.

facts: Deregulation, tax reduction and abolition of exchange controls.
1990 government rejected central bank independence; 1989 advocated environmental regulation.
controle.tension: Market price allocation coexists with elected monetary authority and targeted public regulation, not abolition of government money or all regulation.

facts: 1988 backed single market and GATT barrier reduction.
Rejected a protectionist European bloc, defended foreign financial participation.
comercio.tension: Sovereign political nations and border checks are compatible with freer commerce; security exceptions do not imply economic autarky.

facts: 1988 Christian ethical principles and religious education.
Supported national Christian heritage and equal legal treatment for other religions.
religiao.tension: Publicly religious and morally conservative but no clerical state, universal Christian party monopoly or religious discrimination.

facts: 1987–1988 Section 28 and traditional family teaching.
Earlier votes supporting abortion reform and private homosexual decriminalisation supply context.
moral.tension: Traditional norms distinguish public endorsement from private criminalisation; neither generic anti-abortion absolutism nor modern LGBT equality fits all evidence.

facts: 1988–1989 nuclear energy, industrial research and science.
1989 binding environmental rules, biodiversity and tropical forest protection.
1990 vote for licensed embryo research.
tecnologia.tension: Medical research and industry coexist with environmental and bioethical limits; modern AI, implants and designer traits require explicitly labelled analogical inference.

uncertainties: Historical model: no post-1990 personal policy shifts used. Later sources only document facts within the selected period.
Questions mentioning Brazil are interpreted through comparable British institutional choices, not as claims she commented on Brazilian policies.

AI, crypto, facial recognition, genetic enhancement, lab-grown meat and gender terminology are analogical judgements, not recorded positions. Ordinary disagreement/agreement may express a bounded inference; N only genuine tension.
Government minister statements are identified as administration policy rather than personal verbatim quotations.

No Brazilian edition of The Downing Street Years was verified after searches for Brazilian publishers and title variants; conflicting newspaper renderings are not bibliographic proof. Original title retained provisionally in PT; Portugal translation is not substituted as Brazilian.

religionMetadataReview.reason: Public Christian commitments form part of the documented political or religious position; this is not inferred from ancestry or the vector.
